name: Tara Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Tara. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy wine and spirits for Corvino Drinks, a distributor that supplies about 300 restaurants and bars. Most mornings I'm on the phone with vineyards and importers, sorting out allocations, because the good stuff comes in small amounts and everybody wants it. Afternoons I'm checking prices, signing off orders and tasting samples, which sounds glamorous but mostly means spitting into a bucket at two o'clock.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the people. I've got a winemaker in the hills who sends me a card every Christmas, and that's how you get his best barrels, by being someone he trusts. What wears me out is the new ordering system head office brought in last year, which keeps suggesting things I'd never buy. I don't use any of those AI tools, I keep my notebook, and my fiancé Marco, he's an electrician, says I'm the last person under 30 who writes in pen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, nicely. People in this trade buy from people, and a computer can't sit at a winemaker's kitchen table. I don't post much online, but I'd say it at our Friday tasting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, it means I keep my job, which is a relief. But my job wasn't exactly carefree before all this. The ordering system is still there, head office still wants fewer people on the phones, and my pay hasn't moved in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and keep my notebook. I'd keep saving about 250 a month for the wedding, and we've already decided on a small one at my parents' church. I might ask for a raise in the spring, but I'd go in with my sales figures, not a speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, but not easy. I'd still be watching the costs, and watching head office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're getting married soon. How does that sit with your work and money in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We're paying for the wedding ourselves, about 9,000 all in, and we've got roughly three months of costs saved besides that. My father offered to help but I'd rather he didn't, he runs a small deli and he needs his money. So in this picture, it's tight but it's ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said head office already pushes the ordering system. Does that worry you even if AI stalls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, yes. Even if the AI never gets clever, a cheaper system might be enough for head office to cut one of the four buyers. I'd hope my supplier contacts make me the one they keep, but I'm not naive about it.

say: I'd tell colleagues that **people buy from people**, and a computer can't build that trust.
I'd say it at the **Friday tasting** rather than posting anything online.
think: I keep my job, but my **pay hasn't moved** in two years.
Head office could still **cut a buyer** using cheaper software, even without clever AI.
do: Keep saving about **250 a month** for a small wedding at my parents' church.
Ask for a **spring raise**, backed by my sales figures.
Keep my **paper notebook** and phone relationships with suppliers.
feel: **Settled** but not easy, still watching costs and head office.
S0.quote: People in this trade buy from people, and a computer can't sit at a winemaker's kitchen table.
fieldNote: She takes **pride in trust**: winemakers give her their best barrels because they know her.
Even in the plateau she worries about **frozen pay** and head office trimming the buying team.
She's paying for the **wedding herself** and refuses her father's money out of family loyalty.

steps.text: Keep buying by phone and notebook from trusted winemakers
Save 250 a month for the church wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the trade will lose something it doesn't know it has. When the computer orders the wine, the restaurants get the same twenty labels as everybody else. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen, including my manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, buying and booking are right there on that card, and that's me. I think Corvino Drinks goes from four buyers to two, and the two they keep will be the ones who like the system. I don't like it, so I'm probably not one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting more aside, maybe 350 a month instead of 250, even if it means a smaller wedding dress. I'd talk to my father about whether the deli could take me on part-time if Corvino cut my hours. And I'd ask Marco to look at our budget with me properly, every bill, not just the big ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Like the floor's tilting a bit and I'm the only one who's noticed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to if things got difficult at Corvino?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, always. My father, my brother who works for the council, and Marco. I wouldn't go to the government for anything unless I really had nothing, that's not how we were brought up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never used these tools. Would you start, if head office insisted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made it part of my job, I'd learn the minimum to keep my job, the way you learn a new till. But I wouldn't trust it to choose wine. I'd be the one checking every order it makes, which might be the thing that saves me, or might be the thing that gets me let go.

say: I'd warn that the trade **loses something** when a computer orders the wine.
I'd tell my manager that restaurants end up with the **same twenty labels**.
think: Corvino likely drops from **four buyers to two**, keeping the ones who like the system.
I don't like the system, so I'm **probably not kept**.
do: Raise wedding savings to **350 a month** and choose a cheaper dress.
Ask my father about **part-time work** at the deli if hours get cut.
Go through **every bill** with Marco to tighten the budget.
feel: **Worried**, like the floor is tilting and nobody else notices.
S1.quote: Corvino Drinks goes from four buyers to two, and the two they keep will be the ones who like the system.
fieldNote: She openly expects to be **one of the cut**, which puts her firmly at anxious.
Her safety net is **family**: her father's deli, her brother, her fiancé Marco, not the state.
She'd learn only the **minimum of the tool**, unsure whether checking it protects or exposes her.

steps.text: Raise monthly savings from 250 to 350 for the wedding
Ask her father about part-time hours at his deli
Go through every household bill with Marco and cut the small ones

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd probably say I'm not worried, because that's what you say. At work I'd tell the younger ones to keep their heads down and make themselves useful. I wouldn't go online about it, it would only start arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm out of a job by 2028. If the computer can do any thinking work, it can work out wine allocations and prices better than me, and it never needs a day off for a funeral. The tasting I do with my mouth, but head office will decide that's a luxury.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking right away for work where you have to be in the room, maybe a sales rep job visiting restaurants, or behind the counter at my father's deli full time. I'd cut everything that isn't rent and food. I'd keep our savings for the rent and stop adding to the wedding pot for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I don't think I'd say it out loud, but I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Most of your day is phone calls and tastings. Does the gap before robots help you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. The robots come later, so a deli counter or a delivery round stays human until about 2031. That gives me three years doing something with my hands, but it's not a career, it's a holding pattern. And three years go fast when you're paying rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the wedding in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still get married, but in the church hall with sandwiches instead of the restaurant. Marco's an electrician, so his work holds on longer, and I'd lean on him more than I'd like. My mother would say that's what marriage is for, and maybe she's right.

say: In public I'd say I'm **not worried**, because that's what you say.
I'd tell younger colleagues to **keep their heads down** and stay useful.
think: I expect to be **out of a job** by 2028.
My tasting skill will look like a **luxury** to head office.
do: Apply for **restaurant sales rep** jobs or full-time work at my father's deli.
Cut spending to **rent and food** only.
Pause the **wedding fund** and hold savings for rent.
feel: **Frightened**, lying awake doing sums while saying nothing out loud.
S2.quote: If the computer can do any thinking work, it can work out wine allocations and prices better than me, and it never needs a day off for a funeral.
fieldNote: A clear gap between **say and think**: calm in public, expecting job loss in private.
She sees the **three robot-free years** as a holding pattern, not a career.
The wedding shrinks to a **church hall**, and she leans on her fiancé Marco's hands-on trade.

steps.text: Apply for restaurant sales rep jobs or full-time deli work
Cut household spending to rent and food only
Move the wedding to the church hall with sandwiches
Lean on Marco's electrician wage while she finds work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been warned, so it's on us to get ready, not to wait for someone to rescue us. I'd tell my brother and my friends to think about trades. At work I'd keep my opinions to myself, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's the same ending, just later. In 2031 the buying job is gone, and I'm 32 and probably newly married. Five years is enough to change where I land but not enough to stop it happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do a proper food-handling and butchery course at the college in the evenings, because my father's always said the deli needs someone who can cut meat. I'd keep working at Corvino as long as they'd have me and save hard, 400 a month if I can. We'd still marry next September, small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, but less frantic than the two years. More like a long goodbye to a job I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with those five years that you couldn't do with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can learn a real skill instead of grabbing whatever comes. With two years I'd be stacking shelves. With five years I could be behind my father's deli counter cutting proper prosciutto and maybe running the place when he retires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you hold responsible, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies that build these things, and the governments that let them rush it out. But I won't sit around blaming people. My grandmother came here with one suitcase, and nobody handed her anything.

say: I'd say we've been **warned**, so it's on us to prepare.
I'd tell my brother and friends to **think about trades**.
think: It's the **same ending, later**: the buying job goes in 2031.
Five years changes **where I land**, but not whether it happens.
do: Take an evening **butchery course** at the college.
Stay at Corvino and save **400 a month**.
Marry next September with a **small wedding**.
feel: **Heavy** but steadier, like a long goodbye to a job I like.
S3.quote: With five years I could be behind my father's deli counter cutting proper prosciutto and maybe running the place when he retires.
fieldNote: She still expects to **lose her job**, so the extra time eases panic but not the outcome.
Her plan runs through **family**: an apprenticeship-style skill for her father's deli.
She blames **tech firms and government**, but rejects waiting for help.

steps.text: Take an evening butchery course at the local college
Save 400 a month while still at Corvino
Keep the small wedding planned for next September

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and plenty can change, so let's not frighten people. I'd keep doing my job well. If people asked, I'd say learn something with your hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd half believe it and half not. It's easy to put off something ten years away. But I think by the end the buying is gone, and the question is whether I've got something else by 38.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Corvino for the next few years and watch what happens to the ordering system. I'd keep saving, maybe 300 a month toward a deposit on a house with Marco. Around year three or four, if it's clearly coming, I'd move to my father's deli for good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than scared. It's a cloud on the horizon rather than over my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Would you wait to see if it really comes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, for a few years, I would, and I know that's the risk. It's how I am with everything new. Marco would push me, he's more of a planner than he looks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger cousin starting out in buying today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn a trade first and buying second. A buyer who can also run a shop or cut meat or fix a fridge will always find something. A buyer who only knows the spreadsheet is the first one the computer replaces.

say: I'd say ten years is **a long time** and we shouldn't frighten people.
I'd advise anyone asking to learn something **with your hands**.
think: I half believe it, and it's **easy to put off** something ten years away.
By the end the **buying is gone**; the question is whether I've got something else.
do: Stay at Corvino and **watch the ordering system** for the next few years.
Save **300 a month** for a house deposit with Marco.
Move to my father's **deli for good** around year three or four.
feel: **Uneasy** more than scared, like a cloud on the horizon.
S4.quote: A buyer who only knows the spreadsheet is the first one the computer replaces.
fieldNote: She admits she'd **wait and see** for years, which is her habit with anything new.
She still expects the **buying job gone** by 38, so her own income is at real risk.
Her fiancé Marco is the **planner** who'd push her to act sooner.

steps.text: Stay at Corvino and watch how the ordering system spreads
Save 300 a month toward a house deposit with Marco
Move to her father's deli full time around year four

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028. There's no time to learn anything, you just take what's going. What would help is proper apprenticeships for people my age, paid ones, at places like my father's deli or the college, so you can earn while you learn a real trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the winemakers. If the computers do all the buying, small producers lose the person who knew their wine was special, like my winemaker in the hills. I think about that more than I think about myself, honestly.

headlineQuote: If the computers do all the buying, small producers lose the person who knew their wine was special, like my winemaker in the hills.
portrait: Tara is a **27-year-old wine buyer** at Corvino Drinks, engaged to Marco, an electrician.
She buys by phone and **paper notebook** and has never used AI tools.
She's uneasy in the plateau about **frozen pay**, and alarmed in the faster AGI pictures.
Her escape route is **family**: her father's deli and a butchery skill learned at college.
Traditional and wary, she'd **wait and see** with ten years, knowing that's her habit.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to learn a trade before the buying job goes.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for people her age, so she can earn while learning a real trade.
